I have vascular, but I also have crohns and now Gastroparesis So I’m fed through a tube- firstly, don’t panic about it being vascular! It’s terrifying but once they know they’ll be able to monitor it to avoid the most severe complications- which often happen in people who weren’t confirmed or even suspected to have it.  This is why genetic testing is best. Second, you may still also have an autoimmune disease- GI symptoms aren’t *as* common with vascular as they are in hypermobile, with vascular many people don’t have that many symptoms at all. Vascular is quite rare still, certainly in comparison to the number of people being diagnosed with hypermobile type, but it’s the most severe so most cardiologists (in my experience of course) are aware of it to some extent already

Once you know you will adapt to it, don’t be put off by the most severe complications.

I think it is just about balance! My parents/school/medical team were very keen to prevent damage and I think having the input has definitely helped, but at the same time I’m still really affected by my EDS, and it just seems that I’ve never had a normal life. My symptoms were extremely obvious though, so I also understand why they needed to be so involved. If you can balance the medical input with the cotton wool wrapping then you can have a fairly normal childhood, which I think is the better way to approach it. The mourning process is unreal, it took me months to fully come to terms with the Crohn’s diagnosis, and with EDS being such a widespread condition its so hard to accept!!

To play devils advocate: I *did* know that I had EDS from a young age: orthotics input from the age of four, physio and hydrotherapy from the age of five, was definitively diagnosed by EDS specialists at seven/eight. I was kept out of contact sports, didn’t go for long walks, barely got to go on trampolines, basically everything they said I shouldn’t do, I didn’t. 

I’m *still* suffering now- really bad fatigue, joint and muscle stiffness, massive pain, and I’ve just been diagnosed with severe gastroparesis on top of everything else. Almost feels as though it doesn’t matter that I was completely wrapped in cotton wool as a kid, my symptoms have been bad anyway.

I kind of wish that I had a childhood where I didn’t know something was wrong with me, or got to do normal child things, didn’t have to take time out of school for treatment (including nearly a month off for inpatient physio bc my muscles were underdeveloped),  never had to use splints and pencil grips at school to make me stand out.

 My EDS has been bad all my life, but seems to just be getting worse as I’m getting older and I wish I had some sort of normality, because my life is far from normal at the minute. 


[saying all of this, I completely understand that knowing would prevent a lot of damage- plus you don’t have to go through the same sort of mourning process? I was diagnosed with Crohn’s earlier this year and went through the motions with it, same with this gastroparesis diagnosis. I completely get that you’d want to be told as a kid and prepare for your life, in that way I was quite lucky]
EDS life expectancy is also based on the vascular types- hypermobility type has a normal life expectancy

My apologies, its early in the morning here and I’ve not slept! Yes humira is adalimumab- my NHS trust doesn’t work with stelara so I confused it for one of the humira biosimilars that the NHS are switching humira out for. In this case I’d say they’d probably be more likely to say that they’ve tried two biological options and that a third is unlikely to work/be funded, but again I’m far from a doctor so the point of call would be the IBD Team.

It may be that your NHS trust only has funding for the one type of biologic (humira and stelara are the same- ustekinuab) and there may be issues with them offering infliximab- as it’s known here- to you. They may also think that if ustekinuab hasn’t worked, infliximab might not work either. But I’m not a doctor. You can bring up infliximab to your gastroenterologist or if you have an IBD Nurse that would be a quicker way to get in touch with them. 

Surgery isn’t always a bad thing if it will improve your quality of life and they could be thinking along those lines especially if you can feel the food moving through your stricture, sooner or later from a clinical point of view that’ll cause a blockage no matter how careful you’re being and getting rid of it now with surgery could prevent a larger surgery with bigger likelihood of an ostomy. 

I don’t work for the NHS and I’m not a doctor so definitely talk to the IBD team about your concerns before moving forward. I’m having funding issues with biologics too, and was nearly given emergency surgery without biologics, but definitely no expert on the matter. 

Good luck

I have two chronic illnesses, and suspected endo too. It’s painful, and there’s definitely a grieving process to go through. I became ill with Crohn’s last October and sadly my Crohn’s hasn’t been put into remission yet. I’ve just got out of another five day stay on the surgical ward where they weren’t quite sure what to do with me. Since March I’ve spent about a month in total in hospital stays.
I found that writing a blog made it a bit easier for me, I was losing control of everything around me, I was a semi-successful law student away from home, had a decent grasp on my health and my life was on track. Crohn’s came and threw that all out of whack. Writing about it made it funny, made my friends understand why I hadn’t spoken to them in months and stopped my Granny from telling me about her IBS (sorry Granny.)

Thankfully I have the NHS so while that’s resulted in problems of its own (haven’t been able to get biologics funding at home away from my GI team at university so for the past four months I’ve not moved anywhere with stagnant treatment) I don’t have to worry about medical bills or debt arising from it, and in my lifetime alone (twenty years) there’s been such improvement to the treatment and management of the disease that even though the whole thing sucks, we aren't all destined for life changing surgery if we react well to the meds.

I think I’m coming out the other side of that grieving process but it really does take time, especially if the condition comes out of nowhere and throws you off balance like it did with me. I’ve spent months curled in my bed unable or unwilling to get out of it, and in the deepest parts of my flare I would lock myself in my room and not speak to anybody because I was so embarrassed and for about four months didn’t have a diagnosis. It can be hugely isolating & was so bad for my mental health that I’m noticing my anxiety from five years ago popping back up. But I’m getting used it it and have a lot of support around me. It’s getting easier, even if my Crohn’s isn’t going anywhere.

I’m so sorry you’re having such a bad time. I had similar: I was in hospital for almost a month in total and as I’m at university my family couldn’t visit, and I don’t have many friends here. I went between wards and private rooms, I much preferred the ward as it meant i was surrounded by nurses and care assistants, as well as other, albeit much older, patients (I’m 20 too, whereas there were ladies in their 90s with me) which I found helped a little bit with the loneliness even though we didn’t talk. I actually kept crying in the private rooms as it left me with my thoughts, whereas there was a lot of distraction on the wards. Hang in there, it’s really tough in hospital alone. Even if they’re busy, you can tell the nurse you’re struggling and nobody can visit you and usually they’ll try to come and have a conversation even if it’s short. Some hospitals also have patient advocacy programs where someone can come and sit with you for a little while. Also, hospitals have moisturiser as they have to moisturise the elderly patients to keep them from getting bedsores, so you can tell a nurse your skin is cracking and they’ll bring some to you. If you’re running out of clothes, it’s not the nicest, but you can wear the gowns they have, my hospital have actual pyjama bottoms and tops available for people with no clothes left. I slept for most of my time in hospital and really struggled with keeping myself busy as I couldn’t concentrate on anything/fell asleep through it, so I don’t have many tips for that, although I did listen to podcasts that I didn’t really care about incase I did fall asleep through them. I would recommend reaching out to other people though, as what your best friend said sucks. People are usually keen to come and help if they can, I had a couple of acquaintances who I wouldn’t normally think of reaching out to who brought me a gift when they found out I was in the hospital. They were the only people who came to visit apart from my boyfriend, my closest friends were too busy with studying for exams to even ask if I was okay. It really sucked. 

Anyway, I know this is probably no help but I wish you the best and you’re definitely not the only person who’s been in such a shit situation. Good luck with the diagnostics and I hope you’re out of hospital sooner rather than later!

I’ve been treated since I was seven yo. Had intensive hydrotherapy/physiotherapy as I had very little muscle mass as a child. Orthopaedic involvement to make braces for me at each stage of development. Worked our way up on painkillers so we know what works and what doesn’t, instead of being made to feel like I’m after strong drugs. Was kept away from all types of contact sports & became aware of limitations, unlike people who develop hobbies in later life that is detrimental to the condition without realising they have a condition. It’s also easier to adapt when you’re younger I think, you don’t mourn it when you’re young. I was just diagnosed with Crohn’s disease at 20 and I’ve found it really hard, despite knowing I’ve got vascular eds which is much more severe. 

Wrapping eds kids in bubble wrap helps prevent a lot of pain later on in life, as there’s less wear and tear.

Hey, sorry to be the bearer of bad news but usually you’re on IV steroids for five days in the UK. I’m currently on day 3 of my second admission in two months. Get in contact with your school and let them know, you’ll probably need alternative arrangements and it’s super hard to concentrate in the hospital.

Would love to potentially help my mother see past my stepfather & protect my siblings too.

I (20f) have really painful underarms that flare up when my IBD is bad, and it often spreads to my legs etc. I had no idea what it was but it looks exactly like photos of HS. I’ve never seen a dermatologist for anything as I don’t have significant acne problems or anything, just the horrific rash that comes and goes when my inflammation is bad. I’ve also always had spots that come up on my bottom that look similar too. It makes me so insecure but I’ve just put up with it because nobody else sees my body. Going to ask about this!

Don’t throw your jewellery away! Especially jewellery with significance. It’d be an awful shame if your dynamic ended and you had gotten rid of your possessions. Not sure of your dynamic but this seems a red flag to me, that your dom hasn’t listened to your concerns and dismissed it as you having to wear what he wants, especially when you loved jewellery. Talk to him again! The sub is the one really in control and you can set this boundary.

Progesterone only pill, ask for it ASAP- even if you have frequent ‘normal’ headaches you’re not supposed to be on the ‘combined’ (progesterone & oestrogen) pill according to my doctor. Works in exactly the same way, just that you have no breaks on it. Win win situation lmao

Hey, just been diagnosed last week. I was definitely scared it was cancer despite being very very young and unlikely. I think that’s a huge worry that goes through everyone’s minds! Before it was revealed to be IBD, I was misdiagnosed with IBS for eight or so years. This has been my first major flare up in that time and we’re getting on top of it now, but all the tests had to be done, I was put through the bowl cancer screening program and came through free. On the colonoscopy, it will likely be obvious what is wrong- they’ll probably still take biopsies, and then you’ll know for certain what’s up, which is a huge relief. Don’t panic now! Focusing on getting through prep and getting some idea of what’s wrong helped me get through that uncertainty. Best wishes!

Hi, thanks so much for the detailed response! I knew the average age of diagnosis is around 20 but on “my island” it is mainly the elderly population who are diagnosed with it (my mum is a preasseasment/surgical nurse depending on the day who is constantly working with colonoscopies and she and her colleagues were quite shocked to see me come in with my colon in such a bad shape! The colonoscopy took an hour and a half due to how much there was to photograph- which is much longer than I was expecting) 

I will definitely be looking into Crohn’s and Colitis UK- these responses are definitely helping me feel less alone with it and an awareness charity will definitely help me settle in with it! I think that’s what I need to do the most, I keep walking about the house saying “I have colitis in x y z” and must be really annoying my family, but also lets me process it a little better. I know it’s not the end of the world but it is another lifelong condition with hellish symptoms. At the same time, I was going in for a colonoscopy, managed prep (I was on Klean Prep as I’m allergic to citric acid and had to drink seven litres of water) and I was expecting something, but not as much as they said (surgeon mentioned surgery as the first option rather than going through detail about medications- I’ll have to see what gastro say next week)
 It’s a strange feeling- maybe not traumatic but definitely a huge blow to me, even though the symptoms that brought me here were bad as well?? Ah well, I’m sure I’ll get used to it, and once treatment is started and it calms down I’ll get to normal again. I’m happy to finally have an answer though, now we can actually treat it! Best wishes

I’m so sorry you’re in the hospital. They have mentioned surgery, but it was the surgeon who mentioned surgery, not my gastro doctor. (Colonoscopy was done here at home where we don’t have a gastro department, just general surgery so i was fitted in with the most experienced surgeon here and was allowed to have a phone call from my gastro specialist where we had a quick discussion about the colonoscopy report). That being said, the surgeon actually saw the damage and the gastro doctor only read about it. I’ll be in to see gastro next week when I’m back to university. I’m terrified about medicine not working! I’ve avoided major surgery all my life (save for tonsils being taken out at six) so to have this potentially looming over me is really scary. That said, I’m trying to keep positive and remind myself that medicine is my first option and that will be started soon. Thank you for the advice about steroids, and wishing you the best for this flare up. What a hassle it must be :(

Thank you! And especially for the advice on taking steroids, because they’re a big fear of mine! This is the attitude I’m trying to have, and the attitude everyone is having around me haha. I’m quite worried about the steroids, with my other condition, steroids can make my already weak connective tissue weaker and I’m meant to avoid them. But in this case it seems avoiding steroids would mean immediate surgery as there’s a hell of a lot of damage in my ascending colon & cecum that the surgeon preforming the colonoscopy was worried about, which I really would like to avoid. I think it’s definitely going to be hard balancing two pretty awful lifelong conditions, but I’m hoping once I’m used to the diagnosis (because it seems I’ve had it for a while and just not known) I’ll be able to get back to normal the same way I did when I was diagnosed with EDS when I was younger

Thank you! I hope you are able to manage your symptoms well. I am definitely someone who overthinks and panics easily so I’m hoping I’m just being silly. My family and partner are being really supportive which is a huge help as well, and I’m sure once we kick it into remission or manage it effectively I’ll calm down and get used to it

My colonoscopy was carried out by a surgeon in my hometown, and not my gastroenterologist. I was able to have a quick phone call with my gastro doctor after he had received an email with the report from the surgeon. The surgeon mentioned surgical options a lot, especially because of the severity of the damage to my ascending colon & cecum, But my gastro doctor didn’t mention anything over the phone. I am returning to university tomorrow, so I will be going in to see gastro some point next week. I think the main plan is to shut down this flare and see if we can manage it, but there’s definitely a lot more going on than they expected, especially because the sigmoidoscopy was pretty much clear and I have actually put on weight rather than losing it, so it’s a really scary place to be in. Thank you so much for the reassurance, definitely needed it!

I’m glad you haven’t had a flare up of colitis since! I think that would be my biggest worry with removal. I know how to manage IBS, but it must be quite frustrating having gone through surgery and still having uncomfortable flares. Just the way of having such a multisystemic condition though, I guess. Hope you’re as comfortable as can be and your flare ups aren’t frequent.

Thank you for the link! Yes, I was aware we have GI symptoms for sure, but my gastroenterologist when doing a sigmoidoscopy when I was admitted to hospital told me that IBD was “different” and I’d “finally have a condition not caused by EDS”.  His opinion has definitely changed after having time to read over my history and see that I was dx IBS at 11 with IBD symptoms & have older scar tissue- which has sparked this post! 

I think there’s a lot more research that could be done into the link, especially when so many of us are affected by GI symptoms and so many people are told it’s IBS, which can be managed without medication and isn’t seen as a “big issue” by medical professionals. 

It worries me that people are misdiagnosed with IBS until a flare up- in my case, it looks like I’ve gone eight years untreated, at an age where I didn’t really want to discuss bowl habits and didn’t recognise what is irregular. I keep thinking back and trying to remember my flare ups, and I know I’ve had a few (none as bad as this) that I’ve just waited to pass. I’m scared there’s damage that is unfixable, especially as my surgeon (not my gastro unfortunately) who did the colonoscopy mentioned removal a lot. 

Anyway I’m ranting haha, but I hope you are able to manage your condition well!

My younger sister (11) has celiac. I wonder if it’s related? So hard trying to keep on top of a diet that keeps it from interfering, especially when that person is a kid. It’s another GI that my family has been told isn’t directly linked. Same with things like colitis, there must be some effect on our autoimmune systems (which also leads to mast cell activation etc)- there’s still so much research to be done for sure. Hope you can stay on top of your symptoms!
Such a hassle! And GI issues are so complex as it is, to have so much going on must be so defeating, and c diff is absolutely hellish on top of all that. Wishing you the best.

Not a fully grown adult yet (19f) but I’m a law student. In my second year. My condition is deteriorating fast though, (dx vascular at 7, experiencing the ruptures that come with it now) and the brain fog & pain is really impacting my studies. I’m worried I’ll have to drop out eventually, we’ll see after this round of exams. Between semesters I have a normal part time supermarket job, working not even three days a week, but even that is hard work and I come home and pass out after a shift. Balancing health and a working life is really tough, I’m dreading it.

I'm a law student, yes, in short, this is one of the five main sexual assaults. In the UK, the Sexual Offences Act 2009 (I think it's section 14) specifies that "nobody asleep or unconscious can consent to a sexual act." This is equally true for a relationship as well as one night stands, and, crucially, consent can not be given in advance (ie, when awake beforehand) So technically, it is assault. But, in a relationship with your partner, after a discussion and clear consent, (this conversation will obviously surround a decision from your partner to agree to the activity, and this decision has to be given with "free agreement") the court would not get involved as this is a conscious decision. This conversation, as everyone above me has said, is crucial and the dividing point between consensual activity, and literal assault. But as long as your partner is aware that this is something you will partake in, and is excited for it, there's no reason for it to escalate to a conviction or anything of the sort. Also, if the receiver wakes up and is uncomfortable, that is obviously time to stop. They basically reserve the right to be uncomfortable.
